3.4.1Representational Recasting and Discursive Recasting ​

Representational recasting rewrites a sourced state, information, or model expression, through a named converter, bridging party, or rule, into a new representation directed toward a target scale, circle[3], task, or vocabulary system. When the payload is primarily language, institutional texts, or explanation, it is called discursive recasting. The new representation must retain its parent record and source lineage.

Recasting differs from scale transformation, transformation of circle relations, network propagation, compression, and lateral analogical transfer. These operations may participate in a recasting, but cannot replace the recasting contract. Whether recasting actually changes understanding or action on the target side still requires materials concerning the specified channel. Whether the collapsed differences still provide conditional increments, and whether different orderings fail to commute, are still tested under the existing contracts for scale closure.

A recasting must register at least: the source formulation and context; the target circle and task; the converter or rule and its version; retained elements; permitted changes; collapsed differences; omissions; added explanations; ambiguities; error; the parent record; the path back to the source record; review on the target side; the validity period; and conditions for failure and withdrawal. Without independent review on the target side, the recasting may only be registered as awaiting testing.

3.4.1Note

Understanding this section

3.4.1 Representational and Discursive Recasting

Explaining technical material to another group involves more than shortening it. State who rewrites it under which rules, which qualifications remain, what has been lost, and whether recipients independently checked it.

Representational recasting rewrites a sourced state, information, or model, through a named converter, bridging party, or rule, into a new representation for a target scale, circle, task, or vocabulary system. When the payload is mainly language, institutional texts, or explanation, it is discursive recasting. ‘Recasting’ here does not permit arbitrary changes of meaning; it requires clarity about responsibility for changes in expression.

Parent records and source lineage must be preserved. Readers should be able to return to the original materials to check context, versions, units, conditions, and edits or omissions. Multiple summaries from the same parent record must not be counted as multiple independent sources. Traceability also does not establish accurate rewriting; it merely makes accuracy review possible.

The minimum record can be understood in four groups. Input: source formulation, context, parent record, and route back to the source. Transformation: transformer or rule and version, preserved elements, permitted changes, collapsed distinctions, omissions, added interpretations, ambiguities, and errors. Reception: target circle, target task, and independent review. Life cycle: validity period, failure conditions, and withdrawal conditions. Missing any key item can cause ‘concise’ to be mistaken for ‘complete in meaning’.

Scale transformation adjusts SP and representational sufficiency; circle-relation transformation handles relations between circles; network propagation describes the nodes and edges traversed; compression reduces expression or data volume; lateral analogy attempts correspondences between different objects. These can participate in recasting, but none replaces the contract for sources, rewriting, and target-side review above. Forwarding unchanged may involve propagation without recasting; an explanation adapted to another task at the same scale may involve recasting.

Whether recipients actually understand or change their actions requires material from specified channels, not the rewriter’s self-assessment. Without independent target-side review, record only recasting awaiting testing. Review may compare answers and omissions for the same task, but this guide recruited no actual readers and performed no such measurement, so it cannot claim that readability has been validated.

If collapsed distinctions still change target answers, judgments of historical conditions, or operational results, return to the existing scale-closure and conditional-increment contracts; if different rewriting orders produce different results, check them against the same endpoint task, rather than introducing a new principle exempt from proof. F4 in 4.18.4 specifically reminds us that each stage achieving its local objective does not ensure that their composition preserves the same final objective.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: a locatable source representation and its context exist, and the target audience and task are explicit.

  2. 2

    Transformation record: disclose the named transformer or rule version, permitted changes, and actual additions and deletions; preserve the parent record and route back to the source.

  3. 3

    Semantic check: examine preserved elements, ambiguity, omissions, added interpretations, and errors; conditions in the original material must not be silently upgraded into unconditional conclusions.

  4. 4

    Target review: the target side independently checks the answers required for its task; without this material, record the recasting as awaiting testing rather than substituting internal self-assessment.

  5. 5

    Connection to results: a further claim of changed understanding or action requires actual channels and comparative evidence; source traceability does not automatically establish an effect.

  6. 6

    Connection to withdrawal: recheck when changes in context, version, task, or material exceed the validity period; suspend or withdraw under the predetermined conditions if key conditions are lost or source return fails.

Distinctions to keep clear

Propagation

Information moves along channels and may even be copied unchanged.

≠

Recasting

Rewriting expression for a target task, requiring rewriting rules and independent review.

Compression

Reduces length or volume and may lose distinctions.

≠

Sufficient for the target

Whether the required questions can still be answered; shorter or smoother wording does not guarantee this.

Scale transformation

Records SP, variables, operators, and loss.

≠

Discursive recasting

Also involves source lineage, interpretive additions and deletions, and target comprehension tasks.

Source return is available

Parent material and versions can be checked.

≠

Rewriting has been validated

Still requires preserved elements and independent target-side checks; a link does not make it correct.

A proposal for clearer explanation

A design judgment proposed by the rewriter.

≠

Actual change in understanding or action

Requires actual reader or channel evidence; this guide has not implemented it.

Teaching construction: a complete record of rewriting a technical record as a management promptTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll fields belong to a teaching proposal; the parent record is this example’s setup, not a real archive, and no actual dispatcher participated.

Let parent record P1 specify current two-node loads (9,1), common units, and a threshold >8: a mathematical setup without actual measurement. The target reader is a dispatcher in a model exercise, and the task asks only whether an overload exists. The transformer is defined as ‘example rule v1’: use the total and maximum to write ‘There is currently a local overload; total 10, maximum 9; location has not been retained, so this cannot support targeted action.’ Preserved elements are the total, extreme value, threshold, and model status; the permitted change is the form of expression; node identities are collapsed; the full distribution is omitted; the operational restriction is an added interpretation; ‘current’ has an ambiguous window; error for this alert task is 0. The parent record is P1 in this paragraph, and returning to P1 permits recalculation; a change in time or load invalidates it. The target side has not yet independently reviewed it, so the example provides only a proposed recasting awaiting testing; if used to locate a target for action, its sufficiency claim should be withdrawn.

BoundaryThis shows how to record responsibilities; it does not establish that real audiences understand correctly or certify any system alert.

Mathematical construction: premature rounding loses distinctions for the same final targetTeaching scenario

AssumptionsValues are treated as exact decimal rational numbers; r(0.5)=1; the final target is fixed as rounding after averaging the original values.

Let r round to the nearest integer, with exact halves rounded upward. The source values are 0.49 and 0.50, and the final target is q=r(the mean of the two values). Averaging first gives 0.495, then rounding gives 0. Rounding each value first gives 0 and 1; averaging then gives 0.5, and rounding under the same rule gives 1. Both procedures ultimately output an integer, but the second fails to preserve the predetermined q. Each local step may look reasonable, yet the composition must still be checked for preservation of the common target.

BoundaryThis is a formal counterexample in which premature compression changes the task, not a real-world rate of linguistic misunderstanding; it does not prove that all rewriting orders fail to commute.

CAIB’s examination of a damage-analysis briefing: preserve both the conclusion and what it refers toDocumented case

On p. 191 of Volume I, the 2003 CAIB report examines a briefing used by the Debris Assessment Team. It observes that ‘conservative’ in the heading referred to the choice of test model, not the extent of predicted damage; the important qualification that the situation exceeded the test database appeared at the bottom. This section adds the question of how recasting affects the prominence of qualifying information: a heading cannot simply be carried over while losing its referent and applicability range.

SourceCAIB Volume I, Chapter 7, p. 191Volume I, Chapter 7, printed p. 191, first four body paragraphs of ‘Engineering by Viewgraphs’Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe citation is to the investigation report’s analysis of an actual briefing; this guide has not repeated an audience experiment. Communication problems are not treated as the sole cause of the accident, and the demonstration rewrite is not claimed to have been validated by real readers.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching counterexample: two summaries derived from the same parent record are counted as two independent supports.

What it limitsRecasting adds expression nodes, not independent factual sources; lineage should prevent double counting.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Empirical counterevidenceCAIB’s examination of the damage-analysis briefing notes that ‘conservative’ in the heading concerns model selection, not a guarantee about predicted damage; the crucial information that the situation exceeded the test database was at the bottom.

What it limitsThe actual material shows that hierarchy and omission in presentation can change the qualifications available to readers; it does not justify attributing the accident to one slide alone.

Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume I, Chapter 7

Teaching counterexampleMathematical counterexample: after 0.49 and 0.50 are individually rounded prematurely, the final integer changes from the target value 0 to 1.

What it limitsA composition must be assessed against the same endpoint task; each step completing a different local job does not guarantee preservation by the whole.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Changing ‘the model applies within the measured range’ to ‘the result is safe’ adds a conclusion the original did not warrant; this is a substantive semantic overreach, not ordinary simplification.
  • One cannot retain only sources supporting favorable conclusions while deleting uncertainty, applicability ranges, or failure conditions; the existence of a parent record cannot compensate for misleading body text.
  • Independent target-side review also has a defined scope; a single review cannot be generalized to every audience, language, task, and future version.
  • Order effects must hold the same final objective, units, and error standard constant; different answers to two different tasks cannot masquerade as a finding of noncommutativity.
  • Communication barriers in an actual case do not prove that one document format necessarily causes accidents; technical tools, organizational processes, and other causes cannot be replaced by a single formatting story.

Scope and open questions

A primary investigation concretely analyzes semantic qualifications and hierarchy in an actual technical briefing, directly addressing source expression, collapsed distinctions, and the target task; no current general effect size is inferred.

  • The demonstration recasting in this guide has not received independent review by actual target readers and remains awaiting testing; claims about user understanding or action effects before deployment require separate authorization and actual material.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Is forwarding the same file unchanged to another department necessarily recasting?

  2. 2

    Is a summary accurate merely because it includes a link to the original?

  3. 3

    The rewriter finds the text fluent, but the target side has not reviewed it; how should it be recorded?

  4. 4

    Why must q be fixed first in the rounding example?

  5. 5

    Can a briefing that downplays risk information establish that ‘slide format necessarily causes accidents’?

Is forwarding the same file unchanged to another department necessarily recasting?

Not necessarily. It is at least propagation; without rewriting expression for the target task, a change of recipient alone does not establish fulfillment of the recasting contract.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Is a summary accurate merely because it includes a link to the original?

No. Context, version, preserved elements, omissions, added interpretations, and the target task must also be checked; a link only provides a route back.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

The rewriter finds the text fluent, but the target side has not reviewed it; how should it be recorded?

Recasting awaiting testing. A design and expectations may be supplied, but effects on understanding or action cannot be claimed as established.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why must q be fixed first in the rounding example?

Otherwise, the two procedures may simply perform different tasks, and different answers do not show which one failed. Fixing q makes it possible to identify the distinction lost by the second procedure that was needed for the common endpoint.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Can a briefing that downplays risk information establish that ‘slide format necessarily causes accidents’?

No. The case supports a problem with qualifying information in a specific expression; tool format, transmission chain, decisions, and accident causation still require separate checks.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

3.5The 11 Universal Structural Primitives ​

3.5Note

Understanding this section

3.5 Eleven Universal Structural Primitives

This heading opens eleven distinct question cards: how an object is registered, where its boundaries lie, what is observed, what implements it, and how change, return, and history enter an explanation. The cards connect, but none can answer for another.

Chinese source lines 519–520 contain only the parent heading, with no additional proposition or proof. This unit explains the reading entry point; the actual definitions are in 3.5.1 through 3.5.11, each explained independently below. This navigation does not replace the eleven sections themselves.

Following this part’s introduction and the account of composition in 3.6, U01–U03 concern candidate objects and observation; U04–U06 concern implementation locations, relations, and transmission; U07–U10 concern return, environment, load, and history; U11 concerns the operating ranges of the same object and loss of identity. This grouping assists reading; it is not a universal sequence of life stages from the first group to the fourth.

Here, ‘primitives’ are positions that explanation needs to distinguish. This does not mean that all eleven are indivisible physical entities, nor does it claim uniqueness, independence, or completeness. A sufficient subset may be selected for a task, with the effects of omissions explained; fields that are inapplicable, unknown, unobservable, or protectively undisclosed must be distinguished explicitly, not automatically filled in.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Textual premise: this parent section contains only a heading; definitions must be read in the subordinate H3 sections. The guide writer’s additions cannot be treated as original text from the parent section.

  2. 2

    Reading connection: first distinguish the responsibility of each question card, then return to the particular task and select the necessary interfaces.

  3. 3

    Limit on conclusions: listing eleven names does not prove that any real object satisfies them, or that they are mutually independent or exhaust the world.

Distinctions to keep clear

Contents navigation

Tells readers which questions are asked next.

≠

Substantive evidence

Supports particular object, channel, or historical claims; it cannot be obtained by counting contents entries covered.

Interface composition

Different positions may supply inputs to each other.

≠

Mutual proof

Inferring the others’ existence from one’s existence is not permitted by the original text.

Teaching construction: choose cards by question firstTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOnly the responsibilities of two invented tasks are compared; there is no real object or experiment.

Suppose the current task merely describes a registered configuration at a particular moment. Checking the object, boundaries, and observation can support a description. If the next claim is that the object has learned a rule, material on return, retention, invocation, and task results is required; the static checklist cannot be reused to declare successful learning.

BoundaryThis does not claim that any task invariably needs only the first three items; specific omissions still require review.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary case: a table fills all eleven columns with ‘present’ and immediately declares the model complete and the organization mature.

What it limitsFilling fields is not validation, and the number of primitives is not a scale of stages or value.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Do not use ‘more primitives employed’ as a score for a more advanced object, a more correct explanation, or a more justified action.
  • This heading contains no separate empirical proposition; no historical story is invented to prove the elevenfold classification.

Scope and open questions

This unit is a heading-only navigation entry with no independent empirical assertion; historical facts are not forced into it. It has no separate relation diagram, avoiding duplication of the composition diagram in 3.6; the eleven sections below each provide substantive diagrams.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Once the parent heading is understood, can the eleven sections be skipped?

  2. 2

    If a task uses only some primitives, how can arbitrary omission be avoided?

Once the parent heading is understood, can the eleven sections be skipped?

No. The parent heading is only a reading entry point; each section distinguishes different evidentiary responsibilities and conditions of inapplicability.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If a task uses only some primitives, how can arbitrary omission be avoided?

State the target and required inputs, and explain item by item why an omission does not affect that conclusion, or leave unresolved the part that cannot consequently be answered.

3.5.1U01 Candidate Object Interface ​

U01 registers only the D0 candidate object S*=<B,X,R,I,T,SP,K> and its traceability across scales. N0 is frozen in a specific G-instance; completing U01 does not guarantee in advance that G1 holds.

The function of U01 is to turn an object of intended study into a traceable input: the object-instance ID and the seven D0 fields must be complete, with a root-instance contract then established when applying for formal root-instance support. It permits soft boundaries, short-duration objects, forms with multiple centers, and distributed forms, but does not presuppose that the groupings in these forms bring a gain. U01 is not applicable to purely metaphysical objects for which the declaration of empirical fields is refused. Completing U01 permits only the registration of candidate objects and the generation of questions awaiting testing; it does not generate value, responsibility, choice, or authorization to act.

3.5.1Note

Understanding this section

3.5.1 U01 Candidate object interface

First give what you want to study a traceable identity and state clearly “what I mean.” Short duration, blurred boundaries, or the absence of a single center are all compatible with proposing a candidate, but these forms do not themselves guarantee usefulness.

U01 invokes D0's seven fields and adds an object-instance ID so that subsequent material, versions, and tests can refer to the same candidate. B, X, R, I, T, SP, and K must all be registered. Completeness means no silent gaps, not forcibly converting unknowns into knowns. Explain separately how unknown fields limit the question. Scale traceability means source, target, and identity remain traceable after changes in representation or scale.

Soft boundaries may be expressed through membership rules, probabilities, or thresholds, with sensitivity stated. Short-lived objects require short windows and identity criteria. Multicentered and distributed objects require actual connections and interfaces to be registered, not a supreme coordinator invented afterward. They are neither excluded for failing to resemble rigid entities nor automatically valid because they sound open or advanced.

Create a root-instance contract when entering a specific empirical judgment. Freeze N0 in the G-instance rather than inserting it into the object vector. A claim to G1 grouping gain requires the corresponding comparison. Completion of U01 permits only candidate proposals and questions for testing. Reliable domain records can still support their own facts about the object, but the interface cannot directly generate a unified will, value, responsibility, or authority to act.

U01 does not apply to a purely metaphysical object that refuses declaration of any empirical fields. “Not applicable” limits only the use of this empirical interface; it does not adjudicate the object's existence, philosophical meaning, or value.

U01 makes object candidates locatable and versionable; G1 tests grouping gain relative to a matched N0. If a school's identity and relations have reliable records, failure of that school grouping to improve a particular achievement prediction narrows only the grouping claim for that task. It cannot erase the school, students, or affected people.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Provide an instance ID and seven fields so that each record and subsequent question has a definite referent.

  2. 2

    Explain the boundary form, time, and cross-scale tracing method, and disclose how unknowns narrow claims.

  3. 3

    For empirical comparison, create a separate specific root instance and N0. Completed registration does not establish G1 or other strong conclusions.

  4. 4

    If the object refuses empirical fields, state that U01 is not applicable. Do not miswrite an interface's inapplicability as philosophical negation.

Distinctions to keep clear

Instance ID

Distinguishes and enables reference back to a candidate.

≠

Proof of existence or validity

An ID only identifies; material is still required.

Soft boundary

Membership may vary gradually or be uncertain under explicit rules.

≠

Arbitrary boundary

Changes with results without rules, making it uncheckable.

Multicentered candidate

Permits distributed relations to be proposed.

≠

Shared will

A stronger claim concerning a human subject, not inferred from form.

Teaching construction: short-lived queue candidate Q1Teaching scenario

AssumptionsAll fields are mathematical assumptions. SP axes not expanded here must still be registered individually in a full application; difficult fields cannot be deleted.

Let Q1 be a virtual queue appearing within five steps. B includes the queue and service node; X is integer length at each step; R specifies exactly 1 item served per step when nonempty; I is external arrivals; T is steps 0 through 5; SP registers applicable axes such as discrete time, single-queue aggregation, and integer resolution, with reasons for nonapplicability on axes lacking spatial/organizational/authorization semantics; K is the fixed queue identifier and service rule. Stopping observation at step 5 does not mean an actual object has permanently dissolved: the short window belongs only to this contract.

BoundaryIllustrates how U01 admits a short-lived object, not G1 gain for this grouping or actual service efficiency.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary: after Q1 receives a unique ID, the author writes “it now has a unified goal and responsibility.”

What it limitsIdentification and seven fields only declare a candidate; they provide no argument for goals, responsibility, or authorization.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The same ID must not silently refer to an object whose boundary, scale, or K has changed. Record versions and identity transformations.
  • When boundary sensitivity is insufficiently established, the candidate may be retained while comparison conclusions are limited. Do not manufacture observations for formal completeness.

Scope and open questions

U01 is an interface for candidate registration. An explicit teaching object explains its registration responsibilities; no universal fact here requires certification by a particular historical event.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Does the absence of an overall responsible person make U01 unusable for a distributed object?

  2. 2

    What does “not applicable” mean when a purely metaphysical question refuses observable fields?

Does the absence of an overall responsible person make U01 unusable for a distributed object?

It may be proposed, but nodes, relations, and interfaces must be registered from actual material without inventing a center. Effectiveness and responsibility remain separate judgments.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

What does “not applicable” mean when a purely metaphysical question refuses observable fields?

It means only that this empirical interface, U01, does not fit; it does not establish that the question is meaningless or the object nonexistent.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

3.5.2U02 Boundaries and Interfaces ​

Boundaries distinguish the inside of an object from its outside; interfaces record exchanges and constraints across the boundary. Boundaries can be permeable, movable, nested, or overlapping; interfaces can filter, delay, convert, or block processes across the boundary. Spatial proximity does not automatically constitute a shared boundary. The existence of a boundary does not imply that the object is closed; still less does the existence of an interface imply that any one party holds control rights. Across scales, the distinction between inside and outside and the traceability of channels should be retained, while allowing boundaries and interfaces to be reorganized. This primitive is not applicable to objects for which no distinction between inside and outside can be declared.

3.5.2Note

Understanding this section

3.5.2 U02 Boundaries and interfaces

Drawing a boundary states what is included this time; describing an interface states how things cross it. Boundaries may leak, move, or overlap. An interface may only receive, without being under your control.

Boundaries distinguish inside from outside; interfaces describe cross-boundary processes. Record what is exchanged, its constraints, and direction. Merely drawing a circle does not establish closure. Filtering, delays, conversion, or blockage may occur at interfaces; their existence and magnitude still require records or tests.

A permeable boundary remains a boundary: inside and outside can be distinguished while exchanges occur. Moving boundaries require timestamps; nested boundaries require identifying the level at which inside and outside are distinguished; overlapping objects allow the same unit to belong to both. Spatial proximity does not automatically make one object, while long-distance connections may cross residential or administrative boundaries.

Cross-scale transformations must preserve the provenance of original inside/outside distinctions and channels. After aggregation, an interface crossing small units may become an internal relation in the larger object, while a former external environment may be included in the object. Record this reorganization rather than declaring that the interface mysteriously disappeared.

An interface is not a certificate of control. Receiving signals, carrying transmission, being affected, having the technical ability to close a channel, and having authority to close it are different things. U02 is inapplicable if no inside/outside distinction can be declared. If a distinction exists but material is insufficient, that is unknown, a different status.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First distinguish inside and outside under the current B and T; distance or names cannot replace membership rules.

  2. 2

    Trace the items crossing each interface and any filtering, delay, or conversion. Claims of actual effects require corresponding material.

  3. 3

    Redraw boundaries after scale conversion while retaining mappings to source-side inside/outside distinctions and channels.

  4. 4

    The conclusion concerns only boundaries and exchange. Control capability and authorization require separate proof.

Distinctions to keep clear

Boundary

The division between the current object's inside and outside.

≠

Closure

The stronger condition that relevant cross-boundary exchanges are absent.

Spatial proximity

Locations are close.

≠

Within the same boundary

Depends on membership rules for the object and task.

Having an interface

A cross-boundary location exists or can be described.

≠

Having control

Technical controllability and valid authorization must be separately established.

Mathematical construction: overlapping boundaries do not make one large subjectTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe finite sets and relations are entirely teaching assumptions, without actual members or authority.

Let candidate A have members {1,2} and candidate B have members {2,3}, with intersection {2}. They may exchange registered information at 2, but a nonempty intersection implies neither A=B nor a direct channel between 1 and 3. If aggregated into {1,2,3}, the former cross-A/B process may become internal, but its original route through 2 must remain traceable.

BoundaryDemonstrates only overlap and tracing, not any actual community or subject.

Snow's record of water obtained across residential boundariesDocumented case

On p.44 of the 1855 second edition, Snow describes a woman living in Hampstead who had not visited Broad Street for months and obtained bottled pump water delivered by a daily cart. This section's new observation is the actual connection beyond a residential boundary: when studying an exposure network, residential distance cannot substitute for an input interface.

SourceJohn Snow 1855，p.44Printed p.44, paragraph about the Hampstead woman introduced through Dr. FraserReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis is Snow's account linking family reports with death records. The lesson does not treat a single case as complete causal identification, infer modern medical advice, or conclude that anyone controlled the entire water network.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Empirical counterevidenceSnow records that a woman living in Hampstead, long absent from Broad Street, obtained that pump's water through a daily delivery cart.

What it limitsDefining water-access connections solely by residential proximity misses cross-boundary interfaces. Distance from a spatial center cannot be equated with absence of relevant connection.

John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera

What does not follow

  • A boundary change may change the analytical representation or the object itself. Check K rather than treating every change as actual dissolution.
  • Overlap does not imply a shared will among all participants, and cross-boundary exchange does not mean all states are shared.

Scope and open questions

A sourced record of water delivery across locations directly illustrates the distinction between boundary and interface. It does not require retroactively assigning a complete G-instance.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If a boundary permits input, does that make it invalid?

  2. 2

    If two sets intersect, does that establish their identity or communication among all their members?

  3. 3

    Does the ability to observe an interface mean it can be closed?

If a boundary permits input, does that make it invalid?

No. A boundary distinguishes inside and outside; permeability is recorded separately through interfaces. Absence of the corresponding exchanges must be checked only when closure is claimed.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If two sets intersect, does that establish their identity or communication among all their members?

No. In the example A≠B, and no direct 1–3 edge is given. Overlap must be interpreted through specific members and channels.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does the ability to observe an interface mean it can be closed?

No. Observation, technical control capability, and authority to close are different fields.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

3.5.3U03 States and Observables ​

States are described through declared variables and observables, with measurement positions and errors retained. A state is the object's registered configuration at a given T and resolution; an observable is a record formed from a state through a measurement channel. Measurable quantities are not the same as the entire state; not having been observed is not the same as not existing; and a record may also include contributions from the measurement process itself. Changes of scale can alter resolution and observables, but variable definitions, measurement positions, and errors must be retained through the transfer.

3.5.3Note

Understanding this section

3.5.3 U03 States and observables

A state is the configuration you want to describe; an observation is the record it leaves through a measurement process. Instruments, questionnaires, logs, and maps each make only some things visible and may also write their own biases into the record.

U03 restricts state to a registered configuration at a given T and resolution, not the object's entire actual state. Observables are records obtained through measurement channels, requiring positions, times, definitions, and errors. An observable may directly correspond to a state variable, or be only a proxy or mixture.

An absent record has several possibilities: the process did not occur, occurred outside coverage, occurred but was filtered, or its record was lost. Retain unknown status when material is insufficient; an empty cell is not zero. A record's existence also does not mean that the object caused its entire value: instrument bias, question wording, or sampling time may contribute.

Scale changes can alter distinguishable states and observables. Compressing second-level records into daily averages may satisfy an averaging task while losing peaks. Changing variable definitions may make identically named columns incomparable. Definitions, measurement positions, and errors must travel with the mapping; otherwise actual state change cannot be distinguished from changed measurement.

This section does not assume that every study must endlessly add perspectives. Additional measurement depends on the target, error, risk, and task-relevant blind spots. If existing data suffice for a bounded question, retain that conclusion without claiming to have observed every state.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First specify target state variables and the observation window, then describe the measurement channel producing the record.

  2. 2

    Check coverage, measurement positions, and errors; distinguish zero, missingness, and unobservability.

  3. 3

    When comparing records, check consistent definitions and consider the measurement process's own contribution.

  4. 4

    Conclude only about targets that can be identified. Transfer definitions and errors along with the records.

Distinctions to keep clear

Registered state

The configuration selected in the representation.

≠

The entire actual state

Cannot automatically be exhausted by finite fields.

Observed zero

A zero value measured under a known protocol.

≠

Unobserved

No corresponding record; cannot substitute for zero.

Record change

Visible values differ.

≠

Object change

Changes in protocol, bias, or coverage must still be examined.

Mathematical construction: the same reading can correspond to different statesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe additive measurement relation is a teaching model without random error; the numbers are not measurements.

Let observation y=x+b, where x is the target quantity and b is unknown instrument bias. For y=10, both (x,b)=(8,2) and (10,0) are compatible. y alone does not uniquely recover x; reliable independent calibration b=2 is needed to obtain x=8. An empty cell lacks even the premise y=10.

BoundaryIllustrates only identification and calibration conditions, not that real errors must be additive or calibration accurate.

Snow's own account of map omissionsDocumented case

On pp.45–46 of the 1855 second edition, Snow explains that original addresses of some people who moved away before dying were unrecorded or unobtainable, so the map could not cover all case locations. This section's new observation concerns the “observation-generation process”: missing address fields affect map coverage and cannot be treated as nonexistence of the object.

SourceJohn Snow 1855, explanation of the mapPrinted pp.45–46, the first three paragraphs after “MAP 1” explaining missing addressesReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsRelies only on the registration and location limitations explicitly stated by the author. It invents no omitted count, negates no located records, and does not treat the map alone as causal proof.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Empirical counterevidenceIn the map explanation, Snow explicitly notes missing original addresses for people who moved to hospitals or other locations before dying, leaving omissions on the map.

What it limitsLocations absent from the map cannot directly be judged free of cases. This does not automatically cancel evidence from the located records.

John Snow, explanation of map-coverage limitations

What does not follow

  • A contribution from measurement does not make every datum distorted and useless. Quantify or bound its effect on the current task.
  • Do not exceed authority to collect sensitive material in pursuit of omniscience. Something can be both invisible and inappropriate to obtain.

Scope and open questions

The original authors directly explain how records went missing, making this suitable for showing states, records, and coverage boundaries.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    May a blank field be filled with 0 to ease calculation?

  2. 2

    If all readings are 10, is that enough to establish identical actual states?

  3. 3

    If a map is incomplete, must all its located records be invalidated?

May a blank field be filled with 0 to ease calculation?

Not by default. Examine missingness mechanisms and definitions. Treating unknown as zero manufactures an unobserved fact.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If all readings are 10, is that enough to establish identical actual states?

Not necessarily. Measurement bias, position, and protocols may differ; the y=x+b example admits different x values.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If a map is incomplete, must all its located records be invalidated?

No. Retain supported facts about locations while limiting inferences about coverage, total counts, or spatial absence of cases.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

3.5.4U04 Components, Carriers, and Substrates ​

Structural realization must distinguish components, carriers that carry causal transitions, and substrates that provide the conditions for realization. A component is a constituent unit of the current object; a carrier is a material, informational, or relational position through which a specified state transition actually occurs; a substrate provides the background conditions that make this realization possible. A given component is not necessarily the key carrier, and the object may retain K after the component is replaced. Identifying a carrier specifies only a position of realization; it cannot give the carrier intent, responsibility, or an obligation to continue carrying. This primitive is not applicable to purely definitional objects that make no claim to empirical realization.

3.5.4Note

Understanding this section

3.5.4 U04 Components, Carriers, and Substrates

The parts on a list, the positions through which a change actually passes, and the background conditions that let these processes operate are different things. Identifying what carries a process does not thereby prove that it has intentions or must continue carrying it forever.

A component is a constitutive unit of an object; a carrier is a material, informational, or relational position through which a specified state transition actually passes; a substrate comprises the background conditions that enable this realization. These are question-dependent roles relative to an object and transition; reality need not divide into three permanently nonoverlapping piles of things. One position may perform multiple roles, which still require separate explanation.

A component's prominence in a system inventory does not mean that this transition necessarily passes through it. Carrier identification requires tracing how a specified input enters a subsequent state; merely observing a part alongside an outcome does not establish that it carries the transition. Disconnection, replacement, restoration, or other material appropriate for identification may help distinguish possibilities, but this does not authorize any real destructive test.

After component replacement, K may hold or fail, depending on the identity criterion stated in advance. Replacing a storage carrier while preserving the required content and rules may preserve function; if K requires identity of the original material, complete identity cannot truthfully be claimed. Replaceability, function, and historical identity must be discussed separately.

A carrier may be human labor or a relational position, but “the process depends on it” is not a normative reason that “it ought to continue.” Intentions, attribution of responsibility, obligations, and alternative arrangements require separate examination of facts, N/O, and relevant permissions. U04 does not apply to a purely definitional object that makes no claim of empirical realization; discussing its actual computational implementation is a different question.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First fix the state transition to be explained, then list components, candidate carriers, and substrate conditions.

  2. 2

    Use material on actual channels to check through which position the transition passes; do not identify carriers by prominence.

  3. 3

    When replacement or scale change occurs, check whether content, effects, and K are preserved, retaining what cannot be confirmed.

  4. 4

    The conclusion is limited to the location of realization; intentions, responsibility, and obligations to continue carrying do not automatically follow.

Distinctions to keep clear

Component

A constitutive unit of the current object.

≠

Carrier

The position through which a specified transition actually passes, which need not be the most conspicuous component.

Substrate

Provides background conditions for this realization.

≠

Sufficient cause

The presence of background conditions does not guarantee that a particular transition will occur.

Fact of carrying

A process passes through a particular position.

≠

Obligation to continue carrying

Requires independent normative reasons and grounds of permission.

Teaching construction: changing the carrier while preserving content—identity depends on KTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe discrete bits and error-free copying are teaching assumptions; no actual device is operated.

Suppose a virtual program has an input terminal, storage bit m, and an output terminal. Its update rule writes the input bit to m and then outputs m. The content of this transition is carried by m, and the program's execution rules provide conditions for realization. If m is replaced with m′ and its content copied without error, a functional K defined as “identical input-output rules and content” may hold; a material-identity K requiring “use of the original m” fails. Both criteria must be stated in advance.

BoundaryThis does not prove that actual copying has zero error, that components can safely be replaced, or that anyone has authority to replace them.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary: someone is the only intermediary in the current communication chain and is therefore required to perform all transmission work indefinitely.

What it limitsMoving from a carrier position to a continuing obligation lacks a normative bridge; alternatives, workload, consent, and authorization must be examined separately.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • All background conditions cannot be listed as equally direct causes; distinguish necessary background, channels, and other inputs according to the question.
  • A carrier in a model is only an assumption; real-world use still requires locating and measuring it. Diagram arrows do not constitute causal proof.

Scope and open questions

This section distinguishes realization roles from normative non-implications. Pure definitions can be illustrated through explicit constructions; engineering accidents or personal obligations are not invented to prove the role table.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If a system has a spare part, may we conclude that it carried this transition?

  2. 2

    Does replacing a component necessarily create a new object?

  3. 3

    Does identifying the carrier also identify the person who should bear all responsibility?

If a system has a spare part, may we conclude that it carried this transition?

No. The existence of a component does not mean that the transition actually passed through it; check the specified input, path, and subsequent changes.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does replacing a component necessarily create a new object?

Not necessarily. Judge by the K specified in advance: functional identity may hold while material identity may fail. Clearly report the criterion used.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does identifying the carrier also identify the person who should bear all responsibility?

No. A carrier may not be an acting subject, and responsibility also requires material concerning control, knowledge, duties, norms, and procedures.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

3.5.5U05 Relations and Constraints ​

A relation is registered as a structural constraint only when it changes what states or transitions are feasible. Relations describe repeatable dependencies between endpoints; constraints narrow the set of feasible states or transitions. Correlation, adjacency, and co-occurrence cannot by themselves be upgraded to causal constraints; a causal upgrade also requires temporal order and a specified channel, together with intervention or a counterfactual. The existence of a constraint does not establish that it is justified, either. Scale transformation may change effective relations, so the endpoints, direction, and applicable window of a relation must remain traceable.

3.5.5Note

Understanding this section

3.5.5 U05 Relations and Constraints

Two quantities changing together is a clue to a relation; a rule excluding some states is a constraint; deliberately changing one endpoint and thereby changing another raises a stronger causal question. A single arrow cannot bridge these three levels.

A relation describes repeatable dependence between endpoints; at minimum, specify the endpoints, direction or nondirectional character, time, and applicable conditions. A constraint narrows the set of feasible states or transitions. Register a relation as a structural constraint only when it actually changes the feasible set; co-occurrence or placement in adjacent boxes is insufficient.

In a mathematical model, rules may directly define a narrowing of the feasible set. In reality, material is needed to support which states or transitions are actually restricted, rather than merely unobserved. The absence of a combination may reflect a small sample, selection mechanisms, or missing measurements; it does not mean that combination is impossible.

Correlation may arise from a common cause, reverse effects, or the measurement process. Upgrading it to a causal constraint requires checking temporal order, specified channels, interventions or counterfactuals, and alternative causes capable of changing the explanation. Temporal precedence helps, but is not sufficient by itself.

Scale transformations can merge endpoints or change effective relations, so a local edge cannot simply be treated as the same causal edge at the aggregate level. The original endpoints, direction, time window, and method of merging should remain traceable.

A real constraint may result from an unjust rule. Confirming that it restricts action still does not prove that it should be maintained; conversely, considering it unjust does not make its real restrictions nonexistent. Description and normative judgment must both remain clear.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    List the relation's endpoints, repeated dependence, time, and conditions; do not substitute adjacency or identical names for a relation.

  2. 2

    If calling it a constraint, state the original feasible set, the restricted set, and the grounds for excluding states.

  3. 3

    If calling it a causal constraint, additionally establish channels and intervention/counterfactual identification, comparing alternative explanations such as common causes.

  4. 4

    Recheck endpoints and effective relations across scales; justification and responsibility require separate normative and procedural arguments.

Distinctions to keep clear

Correlational dependence

One quantity helps describe changes in another.

≠

Causal constraint

The relevant change acts on feasible states or transitions and requires identification evidence.

Unobserved

Did not occur in the sample.

≠

Infeasible

Excluded by a specific constraint—a stronger claim.

The constraint actually exists

A restriction at the factual level.

≠

The constraint is justified

A normative judgment, which effectiveness cannot replace.

Mathematical construction: how a constraint changes the feasible setTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe finite domain and inequality are constructed rules, not estimates from real-world frequencies.

Let x,y∈{0,1}, with the initial feasible set {(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)}. Adding x+y≤1 excludes only (1,1), leaving three states. Here the meaning and effect of the constraint can be checked directly, item by item. Whether it represents an actual capacity restriction requires independent material; mathematics does not judge whether the restriction ought to exist.

BoundaryFormal exclusion is not treated as empirical causal evidence or proof of justification.

Mathematical construction: perfect correlation may still lack the causal edge drawnTeaching scenario

AssumptionsWhat is given is an explicit set of structural equations and semantics for an external operation; it is not real-world data and involves no intervention on people.

Suppose a common input C takes 0 or 1 with equal probability, with X=C and Y=C. Observationally, X=Y always holds. If the model permits externally setting only X to 0 without changing C or the equation for Y, Y remains equal to C and its distribution is unchanged. Thus a common-cause model can produce perfect correlation without this kind of intervention effect of X on Y.

BoundaryThis only refutes directly inferring X→Y from correlation; it does not prove that a particular actual correlation must arise from a common cause.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleMathematical counterexample: when X=C and Y=C, X and Y are perfectly correlated, but setting X alone does not change Y.

What it limitsA causal arrow requires additional identification; the strength of correlation cannot fill this gap.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Not every statistical relation can be labeled a directed edge. Retain an unknown direction honestly; do not add arrows merely to improve a diagram's appearance.
  • Structural constraints may fail under different conditions; do not universalize them by forgetting their window and environment.

Scope and open questions

U05 provides interface definitions for relations, constraints, and causal upgrading. Two mathematical constructions suffice to test the non-implications, without substituting stories for causal identification.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If two nodes have never been observed to equal 1 simultaneously, may x+y≤1 be registered?

  2. 2

    Does a restriction's actual effectiveness imply that it is justified?

  3. 3

    After two endpoints are merged into one total, does the original edge still exist unchanged?

If two nodes have never been observed to equal 1 simultaneously, may x+y≤1 be registered?

Not from missing examples alone. Check sample coverage, selection, and measurement, or obtain independent rule-based or mechanistic grounds for excluding (1,1).

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does a restriction's actual effectiveness imply that it is justified?

No. Descriptions of effects and normative evaluations have different premises; nor may actual restrictions be denied because they are unjust.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

After two endpoints are merged into one total, does the original edge still exist unchanged?

Not necessarily. Trace how the endpoints were merged and whether direction and window remain meaningful, and reassess the relation at the aggregate level.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

3.5.6U06 Flow, Channels, and Transmission ​

For systems in which transitions across components or boundaries are claimed, flow specifies the object, direction, rate, and distribution of resources, signals, or effects; channels specify the carrying paths; and transmission specifies how inputs change downstream states. Capacity, delay, reliability, controllability, and loss are candidate attributes for measurement channel by channel and dimension by dimension; unmeasured dimensions remain unknown. U06 provides descriptive positions, not proof that any particular channel actually exists; channel effects still require a G2-instance. The source, target, and channel must remain traceable through scale transformation, and a channel must not automatically be deemed a responsible party.

3.5.6Note

Understanding this section

3.5.6 U06 Flows, Channels, and Transmission

Knowing which route a message takes does not mean knowing its speed, reliability, or controllability. U06 registers “what flows,” “where it travels,” and “what changes downstream” separately.

When claiming a transfer across components or boundaries, specify the flow's object, direction, rate, and distribution; the channel's carrying path; and how transmission changes downstream states in response to input. Without this information, “resource flow” or “information transmission” can easily become an umbrella term with no checkable content.

Capacity, delay, reliability, controllability, and loss are candidate properties to be measured separately for each channel and dimension. One successful delivery can support the record of that delivery, but not long-term reliability; measuring delay does not also measure capacity or controllability. Unknowns should remain in their respective dimensions, rather than being concealed by an overall label of “effective channel.”

U06 is a descriptive position; it does not make an assumed channel in a diagram actually exist. Existing domain material may support paths or effects within its original scope. Formal support for a channel effect under this framework requires satisfying a G2-instance; completing a U06 form cannot directly confer that status.

When scale changes, sources, targets, and paths must remain traceable, and changes in series connections, parallel connections, shared resources, and delays require rechecking. A channel itself is usually not a responsible party. Even where a person mediates it, a message passing through that person does not alone establish control of the entire process or full responsibility.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First declare the object transferred, source, target, and path; avoid substituting abstract “flow” for an actual channel.

  2. 2

    For capacity, delay, reliability, controllability, and loss, register units, windows, and material separately; unmeasured dimensions remain unknown.

  3. 3

    Claims of effects require tracing downstream changes and comparisons; formal G2 support separately requires satisfying the instance contract.

  4. 4

    During transfer, preserve the lineage of endpoints and channels; examine responsibility and authorization separately.

Distinctions to keep clear

Flow

The object transferred, and its direction, rate, and distribution.

≠

Channel

The path carrying this transfer.

Delivery / delay record

Information about a particular arrival or speed.

≠

Reliability / capacity / controllability

Different dimensions requiring their own material.

Channel description

Can propose a hypothesis about a path.

≠

Support for a channel effect

Also requires actual effects and corresponding comparative evidence.

Mathematical construction: separating series capacity from delayTeaching scenario

AssumptionsCapacity, conservation, series connection, and finite long-term backlog are teaching assumptions, not measured system performance.

Suppose ideal channels A and B in series have stable processing capacities of 5 and 3 items per step respectively, with no diversion or loss, and with long-term backlog unable to grow without bound. The steady-state rate through both segments is equal and cannot exceed either 5 or 3, so it cannot exceed min(5,3)=3 items/step. This upper bound specifies neither each item's waiting delay nor a guarantee that actual throughput reaches 3. If backlog is allowed to grow continuously, short-term inflow at the first segment can also exceed outflow at the end.

BoundaryThis gives only an upper bound for the specified model; it does not estimate real reliability, control authority, or a G2 effect.

Differences in request paths recorded by CAIBDocumented case

CAIB Chapter 6, F6.3-8 states that the Debris Assessment Team submitted an imagery request through Johnson engineering, rather than the usual Mission Evaluation Room–Mission Management Team–Flight Dynamics Officer channel. The investigation judged that this weakened the request's urgency. This section adds attention to the path and receiving context, rather than treating “a request was sent” as the entirety of a channel's properties.

SourceCAIB Volume I, Chapter 6, F6.3-8Printed p.171, F6.3-8Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe account of the path and its effects comes from the accident investigation. This lesson conducts no independent channel experiment, derives no numerical capacity, delay, reliability, or controllability values from it, and does not attribute responsibility to a single cause.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Empirical counterevidenceCAIB records that the Debris Assessment Team's imagery request passed through Johnson engineering rather than the usual mission channels, and judges that this route weakened communication of its urgency.

What it limitsThe nominal existence of a request does not mean that paths and receiving contexts are identical; the report does not quantify every performance dimension of this path.

CAIB Volume I, Chapter 6, request route

What does not follow

  • The average quantities of each segment in a transmission chain cannot simply be multiplied to obtain the overall effect; joint conditions, bottlenecks, feedback, and shared resources may change the conclusion.
  • A path appearing in an organizational chart does not prove that messages actually followed it; actual logs and nominal channels may differ.

Scope and open questions

The primary report specifically distinguishes the actual request route from the usual route, illustrating why the path and the upper limit of its effect must be recorded.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If one message arrives in two minutes, may reliability be recorded as 100%?

  2. 2

    Does a series capacity limit of 3 mean that each item waits 3 steps?

  3. 3

    Is a reporting line in an organizational chart necessarily an actual causal channel?

If one message arrives in two minutes, may reliability be recorded as 100%?

No. This is one delay record; reliability requires an explicit repeated-observation window, a definition of failure, and an appropriate sample.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does a series capacity limit of 3 mean that each item waits 3 steps?

No. Capacity is measured in items/step, while delay is measured in steps; the upper bound does not include waiting determined by queue length and service arrangements.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Is a reporting line in an organizational chart necessarily an actual causal channel?

First check the path the message actually followed and downstream changes. Formal effects also require comparative identification and cannot be obtained from a diagram.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

3.5.7U07 Feedback and State Updating ​

A prior state or output constitutes effective feedback only when it returns through a channel and changes subsequent states, probabilities, or constraints. Feedback is a return relation; state updating is the subsequent change caused by a return or other input. The two need to be registered separately. Feedback can be reinforcing, inhibiting, delayed, distorted, or blocked. Effective feedback is not the same as learning, nor is it the same as repair: for the carrier-learning branch of C3, current updates, subsequent invocation, and task results are checked under §4.5; the historical-increment branch C3-learning/CM-LEARNING-history additionally requires updates that can be retained, repeated rounds, and G3's historical conditional increments (see §6.3); repair additionally requires K*/F* and N/O review. U07 is not applicable to a one-way process with no return channel.

3.5.7Note

Understanding this section

3.5.7 U07 Feedback and state updating

A system may change because it receives something returned from itself, or simply because its external input changes. Even when a return actually has an effect, we must distinguish a one-time adjustment, ongoing learning, and repair that reaches a target.

U07 inherits D2: effective feedback requires a prior state or output to return through a traceable channel and change a subsequent state, probability, or constraint. State updating is a change in a subsequent configuration, which may result from a return or from other inputs. Observing an update alone does not establish a return; U07 does not apply to a one-way process with no return channel.

A return may reinforce, inhibit, arrive late, become distorted, or be blocked. Its direction and value are judged separately: a real effect need not be beneficial, and leaving a lasting trace is not a necessary condition for basic feedback. Compare cases with no return or a blocked return, while also addressing common inputs and synchronized changes.

Effective feedback differs from learning. Following 4.5 and 6.3, C3-carried-learning and CM-LEARNING-carried check the current carrier of the update, retention or continuous updating, subsequent use across multiple rounds, task-outcome comparisons, and the corresponding causal evidence. When the current carrier already retains what was learned sufficiently, additional historical information may add no further predictive value, while carrier-based learning may still hold.

Only when additionally claiming the historical-increment branch C3-learning/CM-LEARNING-history is G3 support for a historical conditional increment relative to an explicitly stated current representation required, beyond retainable updating, repeated rounds, and task comparisons. Do not automatically add G3 because learning persists, or deliberately omit the current carrier to manufacture an increment.

Repair separately asks whether the new state satisfies the predefined K* or F*, and checks targets, decisions, and implementation authority through N/O. Learning can acquire harmful rules; feedback may only briefly change timing; repair may be achieved through replacement rather than learning. Each of the three labels has its own criteria.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First trace past outputs, the return channel, reception, and subsequent fields, distinguishing returns from external inputs.

  2. 2

    Judge feedback effects from comparative evidence; do not attribute them directly from the existence of an update.

  3. 3

    When claiming carrier-based learning, additionally check retention, repeated use, and task outcomes; add G3 only when claiming an additional historical increment.

  4. 4

    When claiming repair, additionally check the predefined K*/F* and N/O; passing one requirement does not satisfy the others.

Distinctions to keep clear

State updating

A subsequent configuration changes, potentially because of various inputs.

≠

Effective feedback

The effect specifically produced by the return of a prior state/output.

Carrier-based learning

An update is retained or continuously updated, used, and affects the task.

≠

Historical-increment learning

Beyond the carrier and task conditions, history adds information or effects beyond the current representation.

Learning

Forming and using an update.

≠

Repair

Reaching the predefined K*/F*, with actual adoption separately assessed through N/O.

Mathematical construction: carrier retention has already brought history into the presentTeaching scenario

AssumptionsFeedback, error-free storage, three rounds of use, and equally probable targets are all mathematical assumptions, with no real participants; current m must not be removed from the comparison.

Let the target bit H be 0 or 1 with equal probability. The model initially guesses 0; feedback provides the error H-0, and the storage bit m is updated to H and retained without error. The same bit is then queried in each of three subsequent rounds, and the output is m. Before the update, always guessing 0 gives an average error rate of 1/2; after the update, each round has an error rate of 0. Given the current m, Y=m is already determined, so adding the history H adds no information about Y. This demonstrates that a model mechanism of retention and use can hold while the historical increment relative to a sufficient current carrier is zero.

BoundaryThis is not evidence of real learning effectiveness or a formal G instance; it only demonstrates the logical distinction between the two learning routes.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching boundary case: a new external input changes from 0 to 1, and a one-way model's output changes to 1 accordingly, with no return of any past output.

What it limitsThere is an update but no return, so U07 effective feedback cannot be recorded on this basis.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleMathematical counterexample: when current m fully retains H and Y=m, the additional historical increment disappears.

What it limitsA G3 increment cannot be made a necessary condition for all carrier-based learning; real carrier chains must still be verified separately.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • A fixed rule can provide effective feedback; the complete absence of retraining does not cancel its effect.
  • One success, one write-back, or one archive is insufficient to establish learning across multiple rounds; a lack of G3 support also does not imply the absence of ordinary learning.
  • Whether the current representation is sufficient requires evidence. One cannot declare the actual G3 increment zero merely by saying ‘the state can always be completed in principle.’

Scope and open questions

This section provides a definitional interface for return, updating, and mechanism branches. A fully explicit bit-storage model tests non-implication without reducing real human learning to an unmeasured bit model.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If a rule changes, must it be feedback-based learning?

  2. 2

    If current memory fully retains what was learned and the historical term adds no further value, can learning be denied?

  3. 3

    Can a feedback rule still count as effective if it makes outcomes worse?

If a rule changes, must it be feedback-based learning?

Not necessarily. Check which return or input caused the change, whether it is retained and used across multiple rounds, and whether it changes the predefined task outcomes.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If current memory fully retains what was learned and the historical term adds no further value, can learning be denied?

No. Evidence is gathered separately for the carrier branch and the historical-increment branch; lack of support for the latter does not cancel supported carrier-based learning.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Can a feedback rule still count as effective if it makes outcomes worse?

It may have an effect under D2; whether it improves outcomes and whether learning produces a net benefit are separate judgments. ‘Effective’ must not be understood as necessarily beneficial.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above
